analysis.one_liner: Adds outpatient prescription drug and insulin coverage to Medicare, with payment limits aimed at drug makers and pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote: after referral to two House committees in May 1991, it went to subcommittees in June and no further action was taken before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made Medicare cover outpatient prescription drugs and insulin for the first time. After a $650 yearly deductible, Medicare would pay 80% of the cost up to set payment limits, and the benefit would be financed by modestly higher monthly Medicare premiums for all enrollees. It also included price controls: government-set payment limits for drugs, price surveys with fines for pharmacies and wholesalers that refused to cooperate, and a rule that pharmacies could not charge Medicare patients more than the general public. The bill died quietly in subcommittee without ever reaching a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — mostly seniors and people with disabilities — who at the time paid the full price of outpatient prescriptions themselves. The help would be largest for people with high drug bills: after meeting a $650 deductible, Medicare would cover 80% of prescription and insulin costs, and organ transplant patients would owe no deductible on anti-rejection drugs in their first year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries with high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: Adds coverage of outpatient prescription drugs and insulin to Medicare Part B, which did not cover them at the time.

After a $650 annual deductible (rising $50 per year), Medicare pays 80% of the lesser of the actual charge or a government-set payment limit; the deductible does not apply to anti-rejection drugs in the first year after an organ transplant.

Sets payment limits tied to surveyed wholesale prices, requires pharmacies to charge Medicare patients no more than the general public, and lets the government fine wholesalers or pharmacies up to $10,000 for refusing or falsifying price survey information.

Requires an annual guide comparing prices of at least 500 of the most-prescribed drugs, mailed to hospitals, physicians, Social Security offices, and senior centers, to steer prescribing toward lower-cost options.

analysis.who_pays: All Medicare Part B enrollees would pay higher monthly premiums ($42.40 in 1993, rising to $53.60 by 1995, several dollars above the amounts then scheduled). Drug manufacturers and pharmacies would bear the price limits, mandatory price surveys, participation agreements, and audits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Part B enrollees through higher premiums

drawbacks.text: The benefit is financed by raising the Part B premium on all enrollees — $42.40 in 1993, $47.70 in 1994, and $53.60 in 1995, several dollars a month above the scheduled amounts — including beneficiaries who rarely use prescriptions.
The $650 deductible is steep: seniors whose prescriptions cost less than that in a year would get no benefit at all while still paying the higher premium.
Coverage excludes drugs intravenously administered at home and limits dispensing to a 30-day supply (up to 90 days with the Secretary's approval), which could inconvenience some patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A real benefit with a real flaw. First-ever Medicare drug coverage, including insulin and protection for transplant patients, would have relieved a major out-of-pocket burden; the price-limit machinery was an attempt to keep that benefit from simply inflating drug prices. But the design front-loads costs: a $650 deductible plus higher premiums for everyone means the benefit mostly helps sicker, higher-spending beneficiaries, and the price controls would have drawn fierce industry resistance in implementation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, sent to their health subcommittees the following month, and never received a markup or vote before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark (D-CA) introduced the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Act on May 30, 1991, and it was referred jointly to the Committees on Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce.

The CRS summary describes a Part B benefit covering outpatient prescription drugs and insulin, with a $650 deductible, 80% federal payment, government payment limits, and financing through higher Part B premiums.
On June 10, 1991 the bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, and on June 28 to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health — the last recorded actions.
No committee vote, floor action, or companion Senate activity appears in the record; the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers and pharmacies were spared the bill's payment limits, price surveys, and charging restrictions. Medicare beneficiaries gained nothing: they continued paying full price for outpatient prescriptions, a gap that lasted until a Medicare drug benefit was finally enacted in 2003 and took effect in 2006.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and pharmacies; seniors kept paying cash

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split is unknown; notably, the committees that buried the bill were chaired by Democrats of the sponsor's own party, and the bill drew only 3 cosponsors — all Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would pay for drugs using government-set payment limits based on surveyed wholesale prices, with civil fines for refusing the surveys, and would publish annual price comparisons for 500 common drugs. Manufacturers' Medicare drug revenue would be capped rather than paid at market prices.

Pharmacies would gain a large new paying customer base, a dispensing allowance ($5 for participating pharmacies), and free electronic claims equipment. But they would have to sign participation agreements, accept assignment, charge Medicare patients no more than the general public, face audits and payment limits, and submit to price surveys on pain of $10,000 fines or program exclusion.
The bill delays coordination of Medicare drug payments with Medigap policies until 1995, briefly preserving room for private drug coverage while a public benefit phases in.
